title: ​What mixed-use developers can learn from theme park design
summary:
Combining retail, residential, leisure and public space does not automatically create a successful mixed-use destination.

The challenge is making these elements work together as a cohesive experience, from pedestrian circulation and sensory design to service infrastructure and long-term operations.

For BRPH, this means drawing on experience across themed entertainment, civic architecture and aerospace.

blooloop speaks with Matthew Flores, chief creative leader, and Tim Campbell, master planning and urban design leader, about how integrated master planning can create distinctive public spaces while meeting the practical and commercial demands of development.

​Designing for a sense of place


BRPH believes that successful placemaking starts with how people feel and interact within a space. Emotional connection can help turn a collection of different uses into a destination with a recognisable identity.


Flores sums up the principle with a quote from Maya Angelou: “People will forget what you said, they'll forget what you did, but they'll never forget the way you made them feel.”

He adds: "And I think the same is true in the built environment. The emotional connection we have with the space around us gives us a sense of place that can reinforce, or even shape, new behaviours and how we experience it.

“We can design in a way that appeals to all the senses, and we can take this collection of different spaces and create one overarching theme.”

BRPH also draws on the concept of the third place, developed by sociologist Ray Oldenburg to describe informal social settings beyond home and work where people gather and build community.

Flores says these shared spaces are central to a successful destination.

“The third place is that social fabric that stitches our community together. It could be a coffee shop, an auditorium, an amphitheatre, or a park. But it's that sort of negative space, or the space in between, that really identifies the space and gives the community an identity—something that people really latch onto.

He explains BRPH has applied this approach across the different markets it serves, reflecting the breadth of its work in Florida.

In practice, this means treating plazas, promenades and gathering areas as integral parts of the master plan rather than leftover spaces between buildings.

​Applying theme park thinking to master planning


Theme park design offers lessons for mixed-use master planning, from visitor journeys and arrival sequences to the relationships between individual spaces. Campbell explains how this can encourage exploration and activity:


"We understand that the primary journey provides guests with multiple opportunities for exploration, and learning to plan at scale is key. That means understanding pedestrian arrival modes and decision points, and how the relationship between anchors creates activity and synergy that drives them both.

“The plan has to reflect these spaces, and each space has to have a meaning. That's one of the things I’ve learned about the theme parks: even the smallest spaces and the space in between have meaning.”

In mixed-use developments, the unifying idea may come from the local context rather than established intellectual property, Campbell explains:

“In the case of mixed-use entertainment, this could be a theme or a sense of place that we're trying to create with these uses.”

That identity must inform the master plan from the outset, shaping arrival sequences, sightlines, pathways and gathering points.

"From a master planning standpoint, we translate that story into the actual spaces through the arrival sequence. Right from the beginning, we give guests something interesting to look at and something to get excited about, whether it's a gateway or a special path that leads you to a destination. We create little nodes and edges.

“You really have to look at the balance of spaces. You have to look at the infrastructure, environmental components, operations, and, most importantly, the site's economic sustainability, and understand the marketplace.

“The narrative gives us meaning, but it also has to make the place work. That's our job as designers: to help clients through this process of understanding and getting the right demographic data and details of the marketplace in that area.”

Flores says creative and technical considerations should be integrated from the outset: “Things like concept, story, and ultimately human experience aren't segregated or different from circulation and flow. When we experience a space, we experience all of that together. So why design it separately?

“We want to think of all of that as one cohesive experience."


This also means establishing a deliberate rhythm across the site, balancing active areas with quieter spaces where visitors can rest and relax. As Campbell explains, the aim is to encourage exploration while ensuring the development remains practical and commercially viable.

"We look to create a hierarchy and a rhythm to the place, a sequence similar to a theme park, but letting people explore, find new places in the environment, and have places for entertainment, relaxing, and shade," says Campbell.

​Designing for the senses


Temperature, sound, lighting and scent all influence how people experience a place.

Flores says these sensory considerations should inform design from the outset: "We have to remind ourselves that people don't experience places through images or drawings, even though that's how it starts."

"Sound can create a sense of calm, but it can also create a sense of energy depending on what it is, whether it's trickling water or music. Upbeat music or classical music can transform a space in a really powerful way.

"And I think smell is one of those undervalued, overlooked senses often. If you smell barbecue, Italian food, or jasmine as you walk through a space, smells often put us back in another place. It's associated with memories. So that can be a really powerful way to design.”

Climate and comfort are equally important, particularly in outdoor environments. As Flores explains: “Whether it's shade in Florida or space heaters in Boston, those are really powerful ways to design and think about the human as they interact with the space.”

Campbell explains how landscaping, water and shade translate these principles into practice:

"Every space has to have a meaning and engage the senses of some type. We bring water into spaces to create an ambience. We provide shade gardens and consider microclimates so guests can sit and relax. We look at landscaping and how that helps solidify and bring the property together.”

Architectural details can also create a distinctive identity. Bespoke gateways and entrances reinforce a development's character and visually connect its areas.

​Bringing dining and retail into the experience


Dining and retail can connect commercial activity with public life, encouraging people to gather and spend time in a destination. Flores sees communal dining as a particularly important part of that experience.

"Eating together is something I've been thinking about a lot lately. The idea of smell, food, and eating together creates a very human experience, and it can't just be replaced with technology. In a world where we are questioning the authenticity of everything we see, it's still nice to have those moments."


“We think about food and beverage and this idea of community and eating together as a really important part of these mixed-use spaces because of that irreplaceable human activity.

“F&B integration needs to meet a lot of different needs, giving people choice; the opportunity to eat on the go, have a place of pause, or enjoy a five-star experience.”

Campbell cites Margaritaville Resort Orlando and the adjacent Sunset Walk entertainment district as an example of how a unifying concept can shape dining, retail and public space.

"I helped with the original storyline of the project, and our whole concept was to bring the beach to Orlando. We went to great lengths, even creating a separate landscape code that would allow us to use tropical plants in Osceola County. We carried that theme throughout, incorporating it into dining and retail so even the restaurants felt tropical.

“The dining creates a ring around the entertainment spaces and grand lawns, designed so people can transfer into these event spaces while watching the action from the retail and restaurants. It gives people that vitality and energy they look for in an evening out.”

The layout brings restaurants, retail and event spaces into a shared environment, allowing commercial activity and public programming to support one another.

​Planning for seamless operations


Deliveries, waste collection and utilities must be integrated into a mixed-use master plan from the outset. On constrained urban sites, this is particularly important where service routes intersect with public spaces.

Campbell explains why back-of-house planning needs to come first: "I can tell you that if you don't start with your back-of-house, your service, and understanding your utilities, you're in for a long readaptive use struggle.

"You always start with figuring that out because you have to leave room for it, and you want to make it work so the public and guests don't intermix with the back-of-house. Whether in an urban situation where deliveries must happen at night, that separation is critical."


“Hiding infrastructure underground and leaving utility chases extra wide, so next year when fibre optic cables or new technologies arrive, you can change them without tearing up the streets, is essential.

“Back-of-house is not separate from the experience because it makes the experience better for the guest. But guests shouldn't see trash trucks rolling down the street in the middle of the day or street sweepers operating while they're trying to have a good time.

“It's common sense, but a lot of people overlook it.”

Flores describes the challenge of balancing service requirements with the visitor experience: “You must understand the needs of clients and projects, alongside infrastructure constraints like truck turnaround radii and trash handling.

“If you don't plan for it, service operations will wind up at your front door, and visitors will not be happy. We do a significant amount of diagramming early in the project to understand these constraints and create clear design rules that we live by through the remainder of the process."

​Making phased developments work from day one


Phased development allows investment to be spread over time, but the first phase must still feel like a complete destination. Flores says its identity needs to be established from the outset, with later phases building on that foundation.

"The identity of the project can't be deferred in a Phase One scenario. We want that identity to be felt on Day One, and future phases can enrich and expand that experience.


“We don't ever want it to feel unfinished. It should feel alive and adaptable.

“One strategy is to establish an anchor that grounds the community right away, like a third-place park area, getting that in place before completing other surrounding spaces. While that requires initial investment balanced with economic vitality, giving people an opportunity to linger creates a ritual that brings them back."

Phase One must also be financially viable in its own right, while allowing for future expansion.

"We always ask, 'What is our fallback position?' We must design Phase One so it works successfully even if no future phases are ever built. At the same time, we must plan for success by providing logical expansion zones, parking infrastructure, and utility capacity for future growth.”

Campbell says theme park techniques can help conceal future phases and preserve the visitor experience during construction: "We learn from theme parks how to properly screen future phases using appropriate signage, graphic buffers, or visual boundaries.

"The goal is to ensure guests feel encapsulated within a complete, finished mixed-use development, even on Day One.”

​Planning for long-term change


Over a development's lifetime, changes in markets, working patterns, transport and technology can alter how a site is used. Master plans therefore need to provide a framework for adaptation rather than a fixed blueprint.

Flores explains how BRPH plans for changing transport needs and future technologies: “It's never a rigid statement that 'this is exactly how the project is going to grow.’ We create a framework for growth.

“We establish the main circulation arteries, front-of-house and back-of-house divisions, and modes of transportation from pedestrians to vehicles. Today, electric scooters, autonomous self-driving cars, and vertiports are entering transportation discussions.

“We need to think in terms of not just meeting today's needs, but creating master plan infrastructure that holds future technological developments.”


Campbell says long-term master plans must balance a clear structure with the flexibility to respond to change: “I've learned that on a 20-year project, you will likely go through market corrections, extensive community feedback, and massive technological shifts.

“You must provide flexibility within a solid structural framework. Housing preferences change, entertainment desires evolve with AI and technology, and master plans must be managed as dynamic, evolving platforms.”

​Building a lasting sense of community


Master planning sets the framework for a destination, but ongoing programming keeps its public spaces active. Campbell says events and activities must reflect the local market and give residents a sense of ownership:

"The master plan must be economically viable and scaled properly for its market demographic, whether a major metropolis or a smaller regional municipality. To achieve long-term operational success, you must work in a sense of community belonging so people feel the space is theirs. That's why programming is critical.

“At Sunset Walk in Orlando, the programming is phenomenal—they close the central square every weekend for events and feature live music 365 days a year. Whether it's a car show, craft show, or community event, thousands of people gather, frequent the restaurants, listen to music, and enjoy the public realm.

“Bringing the community in and making them feel part of the space is essential."

Flores highlights flexibility as another way to sustain public spaces, using a waterfront park project as an example: "A large part of that success occurs when the community takes true ownership of the design.

"For example, in downtown Melbourne, Florida, where I serve on the board of directors, we are developing a new waterfront park designed for multi-use flexibility throughout the day and night. It transforms from a pedestrian promenade into a public park or an active event space.

“Having spaces that accommodate diverse activities is key to future-proofing development."

This approach reflects the value of drawing on experience across sectors and applying lessons from one project type to another.

"At BRPH, we encourage our teams to work across different market sectors," Flores says. "What you learn from designing a school or a technology hub can be applied directly to a community centre or entertainment destination. By cross-pollinating markets, we think outside the box while maintaining technical precision."

Successful mixed-use master planning means treating the visitor experience, commercial requirements and operational infrastructure as parts of the same process. BRPH aims to create destinations that feel cohesive from opening day, adapt as needs change, and give communities reasons to return.

title: Industry innovations: 15 attraction concepts that were simply not ready
summary:
Recently, I looked at groundbreaking attractions in the theme park industry. Attractions so innovative they did something no one else had done before, either setting a new standard for how things would be done from then on or creating entirely new genres of attraction concepts.

Now we’re going to look at the other side of the spectrum: attractions that seemed to be on the cutting edge, but for one reason or another, they failed.

They often ended because the experience was lacking or, in many cases, the technology just couldn’t achieve the concept's vision. Some fumbled through various operational states for years before closing down forever… and some existed only for a matter of days before the dream came tumbling down.

Listed in chronological order, here are 15 of the world’s most infamous attraction failures.

Flying Saucers at Disneyland, USA - 1961 to 1966


One of Disneyland’s early, short-lived attraction concepts, now mostly forgotten, was designed for Tomorrowland and lasted just 5 years.

The basic idea was to seat individual guests on a lightweight disc-shaped “flying saucer” vehicle that would then “float” very slightly up from the field of the attraction that was full of holes from which low-pressure air was coming.

As the saucers floated above the field, guests leaned or shifted their weight in various directions to tilt the saucer slightly and create movement.

In the end, movement was minimal and created little thrill; overall capacity was abysmal, and the air valve system was very maintenance-intensive, so during Tomorrowland's next planned refurbishment, the Flying Saucers were no more.

A fun side note: many assume the inspiration for the Flying Saucers came from tabletop Air Hockey, but believe it or not, the development of Air Hockey didn’t come about until 1969, and the first game tables were not sold by Brunswick Billiards until 1972.

​The Bat at Kings Island, USA - 1981 to 1983


The story of The Bat at Kings Island needs a little explanation because the park still has a very similar roller coaster in operation today, also called The Bat in honor of its legendary predecessor.

The Bat was technically the world’s first Suspended Roller Coaster from Arrow Dynamics. To describe The Bat accurately, the train was suspended under the tracks, and the cars were designed to swing side to side as the train navigated the course’s twisted track.

Hailed as a revolutionary concept that would change the theme park world, the prototype suffered from serious engineering miscalculations that caused major mechanical issues.

The track was designed almost entirely with unbanked turns, based on the idea that the trains would absorb all lateral forces, creating the intended ‘swing’ action.

The severity of the swinging motion from the fully loaded trains was greatly underestimated, causing the trains to swing to their maximum limits at several moments during the ride experience; the energy left from hitting the end of the arc then transferred back into the vehicles, track, and support structures.

Shock absorption systems were put in place, but were frequently being blown out by excessive force from the ride, resulting in far more maintenance issues than anyone had ever expected, and the trains were in need of constant repairs.

Ultimately, Kings Island decided to give up and retire the coaster.

Arrow learned the lessons it needed to make the design work, passing the concept's success to the next generation, which opened as The Big Bad Wolf at Busch Gardens Williamsburg in 1984.

Kings Island also returned to Arrow to build a functioning version of the ride a decade later, opening it as Top Gun in 1993. Over the years, the park lost the IP license from Paramount to use the Top Gun name, which resulted in the ride eventually being renamed The Bat in memory of the 1981 original.

​Jaws at Universal Studios Florida, USA - 1990 - 1991


Tales of the technical issues that plagued Universal Studios Florida's opening season are well known, but none more than the story of the ambitious Jaws attraction, which designers tried to put guests in a boat with several robotic replicas of Steven Spielberg’s killer great white shark.

Immediately, when the park opened in June 1990, the impressive and highly promoted Jaws attraction proved to be an operational nightmare.

Rushed in order to meet a tight deadline for the park opening, the attraction featured extremely complex and fairly untested technology, all submerged below the water in order to power several massive animatronic sharks that needed to perform high-speed underwater maneuvers, including an actual strike onto the guests' boat.

The original, highly ambitious finale effects sequence had a shark attack and appear to bite down on the front of the guests' boat, dragging them further out into the water.

This was followed by the shark returning for another attack, only for the boat skipper to fire a grenade launcher at it, making the shark explosively return to the water, which was then filled with some ‘meat chunks’ and blood colored dye.

A year later, the ride closed; lawsuits began as Universal spent the next two years trying to save what it could, re-engineer, and recreate new sequences for the parts that failed with equipment that could withstand the harsh water environment.

​Drachen Fire at Busch Gardens Williamsburg, USA - 1992 to 1998


According to legend, Busch Gardens Williamsburg had originally tried to contract Bolliger & Mabillard (B&M) to build the Drachen Fire coaster for them, but B&M was unable to meet the desired 1992 deadline, and instead focused its efforts on building Kumba for the sister Busch Gardens park in Tampa that would open a year later in 1993.

Facing increased competition in roller coaster design from the likes of B&M, Arrow Dynamics was tasked with building Drachen Fire and asked to create a layout and elements similar to what B&M had been asked to do.

The result was the creation of the world’s first coaster with a wraparound corkscrew and “cutback” element from Arrow, but the end result was a ride that many reported as being excessively rough and painful to ride, with guests' complaints about neck and back pain rolling in within the first weeks of operation.

At the end of the 1994 season, Arrow was brought back in to modify the layout and removed a “diving corkscrew” element just after the block brake to try and smooth out a pain point.

However, it was not enough to solve the problems, and the park finally shut down Drachen Fire for good in the middle of the 1998 summer season.

​Deep Earth Exploration at MGM Grand Adventures, USA - 1994 to 1996


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Lance Hart (@screamscapenews)

This is a very rare credit to have in the world of themed attractions due to the very limited time this attraction was ever open at the short-lived MGM Grand Adventures theme park in Las Vegas.

Fortunately, I can tell you about this one first-hand…

Deep Earth Exploration tried to jump on the simulator ride craze of the early 1990s by offering a new twist no one had tried before.

Themed as a special underground, drilling-powered vehicle, these unique simulators moved on tracks through a show building and opened viewing panels to let guests see into a themed world at three points during the ride.

Intended as an opening-day attraction when the park opened in 1993, technical issues and testing delayed Deep Earth Exploration's opening until 1994.

Riders would watch the vehicle approach the station on the track, where it would stop and open up a side hatch for loading.

I can confirm from first-hand experience: one ride on Son of Beast was enough to make you think twice about lining up again, but you know I had to do it. By the end of my second ride, I was hurting in places that I didn’t even know I had.

Many found it a bit too much, and after one ride, they were good… no getting in line to ride it again as they staggered off to find a bench to sit and calm their nerves.

There was nothing unsafe about the experience and no incidents or rider accidents reported. Instead, what did Hypersonic in was a combination of high maintenance costs and bouts of downtime in order to keep the trains running as designed.

Kings Island would be home to the world’s first Giant Top Spin, a supersized version of a popular flat ride concept.

There was also a high-end bit of theming to tie into the 2001 release of the feature film, Lara Croft: Tomb Raider starring Angelina Jolie.

Renamed Do-Dodonpa, the revised attraction reopened in 2017. During the COVID pandemic, reports came to light claiming that the new extreme launch forces had caused a string of rider injuries, including broken bones, between 2020 and 2021.

The park suspended operations for a complete safety review and ultimately decided to close the ride permanently in 2024 rather than try to fix any issues with the revised launch system.

Recently, I looked at groundbreaking attractions in the theme park industry. Attractions so innovative they did something no one else had done before, either setting a new standard for how things would be done from then on or creating entirely new genres of attraction concepts.

Now we’re going to look at the other side of the spectrum: attractions that seemed to be on the cutting edge, but for one reason or another, they failed.

As the saucers floated above the field, guests leaned or shifted their weight in various directions to tilt the saucer slightly and create movement.

In the end, movement was minimal and created little thrill; overall capacity was abysmal, and the air valve system was very maintenance-intensive, so during Tomorrowland's next planned refurbishment, the Flying Saucers were no more.

A fun side note: many assume the inspiration for the Flying Saucers came from tabletop Air Hockey, but believe it or not, the development of Air Hockey didn’t come about until 1969, and the first game tables were not sold by Brunswick Billiards until 1972.

Ultimately, Kings Island decided to give up and retire the coaster.

The original, highly ambitious finale effects sequence had a shark attack and appear to bite down on the front of the guests' boat, dragging them further out into the water.

As the only Giant Top Spin ever built, parts were also hard to come by and had to be custom-made, creating lengthy periods of downtime when something did break.

In 2006, Paramount exited the theme park industry and sold its parks to Cedar Fair, but without the rights to continue using the various IPs embedded in the parks, so the Tomb Raider identity and most of the theming were stripped from the attraction in 2007.

While the attraction reopened in 2008 as The Crypt, the theming and music were removed, and the ride vehicle and programming were modified, resulting in an experience that was said to be mostly just flipping upside-down in the dark.

While the impressive Tomb Raider experience left for good years before, the ride itself lasted until 2011, when Cedar Fair closed it for good and said that the ride system had simply reached the end of its operational lifespan.

Vertigo at Walibi Belgium, Belgium - 2007 to 2008


Doppelmayr, one of Europe’s most respected makers of ski lifts, ropeways, and funicular people-mover systems of the era, decided to try its hand at a unique new attraction concept it called the Mountain Glider.

The Mountain Glider was a gigantic, suspended, roller coaster-style attraction that looked more at home at a ski resort than a theme park.

The first prototype attraction was built for Walibi Belgium and was intended to open in 2007, but severe delays and technical issues during soft-opening tests pushed the full opening to 2008.

Following a major overhaul, the park held a massive VIP grand opening party for the opening of Vertigo, including bringing in Belgium’s own action superstar, Jean-Claude Van Damme, to ride it in front of the cameras.

While the opening event went off as planned, it was said that the Vertigo attraction suffered a major technical breakdown just 11 days later.

After an inspection, Walibi determined the problem was too severe and too expensive to fix, so they had Doppelmayr remove the attraction for good at the end of the season, making one of the world's most unique rides vanish forever without a trace.

​Luigi’s Flying Tires at Disney California Adventure, USA - 2012 to 2015


Stop me if you’ve heard this one before… Disney tried to create an attraction where saucers would float on air not just once, but twice!

Unfortunately, the concept from modern Disney Imagineers failed for pretty much the same reason the original attraction did. It just wasn’t fun enough and was labor-intensive to operate and maintain.

As the tale goes, Disney Imagineers were trying to come up with other attraction ideas for Cars Land at Disney California Adventure. Inspired by the challenge of the old Flying Saucers attraction, they came up with the idea to create Luigi’s Flying Tires, themed to Luigi’s Casa Della Tires shop from the film.

Guests would ride inside giant tires instead of flying saucers that were much bigger, able to hold 2 or 3 guests at a time. The end result was that the tires barely moved, no matter how much the guests struggled to control them.

Disney tried to add a little more fun by introducing music and throwing an assortment of beach balls onto the course, but the Flying Tires were retired even more quickly than the Flying Saucers.

​Ring Racer at Nürburgring, Germany - 2013 to 2013 (4 days, 31 October to 3 November)


This story may sound a little familiar, too, because it involves another attempt by S&S Power to create a record-breaking air-launched roller coaster. This version of the launched coaster was created to launch right alongside the world-famous Nürburgring race track in Germany.

The racecar-themed trains were to launch in front of the crowds at the track, hitting a top speed of 135 mph in just 2.5 seconds.

During testing of the launch system in 2009 (the intended year it was to open), it was said that one of the compressed air tanks for the launch system exploded with enough force to shatter windows in nearby buildings.

To avoid another incident with crowds present, modifications lowered the launch intensity and top speed to 99.4 mph in 2 seconds. Unfortunately, the Ring Racer coaster ran for only four days in 2013 as part of the RingWerk attraction before they opted to close it for good.

Over the years, many hoped it might reopen, as the track and structure remained in place at Nürburgring for the next 12 years. In 2025, demolition crews finally began removing sections of the coaster track, but even today, the large turnaround track element at the far end of Ring Racer is still in place for guests to see.

​Twist Coaster Robin at Yomiuriland, Japan - 2014 (1 day, 14 March)


The full story of what happened with Twist Coaster Robin in Japan remains somewhat of a mystery, as it is said the coaster was open to the public for less than a full day before being closed for good.

Built by the Japanese company Sansei, the new coaster concept was said to be based on S&S Power’s designs for the El Loco roller coaster system, which S&S had built six of between 2008 and 2014 at various parks around the world.

Sansei had purchased a 77.3% ownership stake in S&S in 2012 and went on to purchase the rest of the ownership shares in 2014, so it seems they set about making a Sansei-branded version for Yomiuriland.

According to various reports, only a few hours after the grand opening of Twist Coaster Robin, a major incident was said to have taken place. Various reports described the incident as a car on the lift hill detaching from the lift and rolling backwards about 5 to 10 feet down the lift before crashing into a second car sitting in the station.

While passengers were said to be on board, thankfully there were no reported serious injuries from the incident.

Later investigations reported that the incident occurred because of a flaw in the design of a new custom anti-rollback device installed to be quieter than the normal version used on the S&S models.

The ride closed immediately, and though they spent about two years working out possible design modifications to reopen it, Yomiuriland ultimately opted not to reopen Twist Coaster Robin and had it demolished and scrapped in 2016.

​Submarine Quest at SeaWorld San Diego, USA - 2017 to 2017


This is one of the most curious entries on this list, as this short-lived attraction wasn't high-speed or high-thrill, nor was it cutting-edge. It was meant to be a slow-moving attraction that traveled through a few indoor segments, but most of it ran on an elevated outdoor trackway.

Described as an open-air dark-ride concept, the final version of the attraction seemed to have some design conflict. Concept art shown before building the attraction featured almost entirely views of the ride passing through enclosed segments past aquarium-filled animals, in an attempt to create an educational experience-based attraction.

The final, somewhat value-engineered concept instead featured mostly outdoor track segments and a vehicle loaded with touchscreens that prompted riders to play games on the screens during the ride, rather than asking them to view the scenery along the way for much of the journey.

According to riders, the touch screens not only suffered from frequent glitches, but the glare from the sun in the mostly outdoor layout made them very difficult to see. In the end, most guests deemed the attraction un-fun and un-educational, and it served no real purpose.

With no explanation from SeaWorld San Diego, the attraction was simply shut down for good after running for less than a year. The park removed the attraction's elevated structure entirely by 2021, likely during one of the park’s state-mandated COVID pandemic shutdowns.

Do-Dodonpa at Fuji-Q Highland, Japan - 2017 to 2021


The tale of this ride is long and interesting… Do-Dodonpa first opened in 2021 as “Dodonpa”, the world’s second S&S Thrust Air coaster.

While the Hypersonic XLC ride that opened at Kings Dominion this same year was an expanded version of the prototype test concept, Dodonpa took everything S&S learned from the prototype and refined it into an even bigger and more majestic full circuit launched coaster, able to reach a record-breaking launch speed of 106.9mph (182km/h) in just 1.8 seconds.

Go on…read those numbers again and remember that Hypersonic reached a top launched speed of just 80mph in 1.8 seconds. To this day, I don’t think any other amusement park attraction has come close to Dodonpa's lofty acceleration goal.

In the world of launched coasters, the current king is still Formula Rossa at Ferrari World, which takes nearly 5 seconds to reach its top speed of 149mph, and while the new Falcon’s Flight at Six Flags Quiddia City can achieve a top speed of 155.3 mph, it uses a magnetic launch system to boost the speed of a moving train as it is dropped down the side of a cliff.

So, Dodonpa's power is still considered legendary.

In late 2016, Fuji-Q closed Dodonpa to make major changes to the ride. The well-known top hat element was removed and replaced nearly a year later by a nearly 50-meter-tall vertical loop inversion.

The launch system was also retooled and upgraded in order to reach a new, even faster top speed of 111.8mph (180 km/h) in just 1.56 seconds.

Renamed Do-Dodonpa, the revised attraction reopened in 2017. During the COVID pandemic, reports came to light claiming that the new extreme launch forces had caused a string of rider injuries, including broken bones, between 2020 and 2021.

The park suspended operations for a complete safety review and ultimately decided to close the ride permanently in 2024 rather than try to fix any issues with the revised launch system.

title: D-Tex Visual expands range of AI sensors to the theme park sector
summary:
D-Tex Visual, a company that focuses on the development of AI sensors for safety and maintenance purposes within the theme park industry, has drawn on lessons from beyond the sector to develop a series of monitoring solutions that enhance preventive maintenance, early warning, and data collection.

These include the G2i, the G2iX, the G2T, and the G2R, which together make the most powerful condition monitoring solution available for the themed environment.

Applications include monitoring safety restraints and coaster car and/or track elements, as well as unparalleled maintenance insight.

"From the early days of developing the Bolt-iT AI sensor, we have continued to push the capabilities of our patented technology in various fields," says Lee Hollinshead, founder, D-Tex Visual.

"Although what we do is very new to the theme park industry, it has been more readily accepted in industry, allowing us to create a complementary range of Bolt-iT variants."

Comprehensive range


The most recent addition to the lineup is the G2iX, which can extract an unprecedented amount of data from D-Tex Visual's newly developed coded field technique.

The sensor offers a level of detail never before seen on components such as coaster restraints, using 3D plotting and extracted data such as angle, standoff, runout, and wobble for every rotational cycle.

This makes it possible to visualise the part's actual path in real-time and identify every tilt and bump while it operates, even on fast-moving parts.

In addition to safety implications, this also provides significant insights to support maintenance.

This model offers double the processing power of the compact G2i, which accurately measures belt RPM and reports anomalies using multi-layered sensing and edge AI while running power and data over the industry-standard CAN network.

Also in the series is the G2T, a battery-powered transmitter that works with the CAN-powered receiver, the G2R. Together, these components continually transmit data from multiple internal detectors across air gaps, where cabling is impossible because of difficult-to-access, fast-moving parts.

The G2R also offers the same built-in monitoring as the smaller G2i, and can also receive data from the self-contained Bolt-iT sensor.

This range offers a unified solution that can be rapidly deployed for almost any application.

Reflecting this versatility, D-Tex Visual is now offering its products and expertise for licensing or acquisition to key companies in strategic sectors, including theme parks.

title: Disney set to cut thousands of jobs in latest round of layoffs
summary:
The Walt Disney Company is preparing for another round of layoffs, with thousands of workers expected to be impacted.

The entertainment giant's latest job cuts were first reported by Bloomberg, which cited anonymous sources. They will be made across multiple divisions.

Some managers of the affected segments have been asked to cut expenses by up to 20 percent on an annualised basis.

Disney declined to comment on the latest cuts, which would be the fourth round of layoffs under new CEO Josh D'Amaro.

The Magic of Disney Animation is open at Disney's Hollywood Studios at Walt Disney World in Florida Disney

According to the Bloomberg report, D'Amaro plans to reinvest the savings into film and TV, technology, and the theme parks and cruise business.

Disney is also laying off between 100 and 200 workers across its theme parks division as the entertainment giant continues a restructuring programme.

These cuts are limited to Disney Experiences and are part of an evaluation of the segment's priorities, investments and project timelines.

Before that, Disney eliminated nearly 300 workers, primarily in the human resources and technology divisions, and separately offered early retirement packages to older employees.

Restructuring at Disney

In April, D'Amaro announced the elimination of around 1,000 positions at Disney as the company worked to "streamline our operations".

At Bloomberg News' Screentime media conference in Hollywood in October, Disney's president Dana Walden said: "There is a need to constantly evaluate how you’re structured.

"It is extremely painful. We’ve exited colleagues who I’ve worked with for most of my career and it is, in many ways, a harsh reality."

Addressing Disney's voluntary retirement programme, Walden said it was designed to give "long-tenured executives agency and the opportunity to make their own decisions around whether the timing was right to leave".

“This evolution, it will never stop,” Walden added. “Technology set their sights on our business, and we must survive, and thrive and grow. And that’s what we’re going to do."

title: Chance Rides highlights the value of face-to-face connections during show season
summary:
Chance Rides, a leading amusement ride manufacturer, is highlighting the value of face-to-face connections during the industry’s busy show season.

With social media and online communication offering more opportunities to connect throughout the year, the manufacturer says in-person events still play an important role in building relationships, exchanging ideas, and understanding clients' needs.

“After 65 years in the industry, we believe the answer is yes,” says Aaron Landrum, CEO of Chance Rides, on whether investing in attending and exhibiting at trade shows remains worthwhile.

See also: Chance Rides at 65: innovation, experience and the next generation of attractions

While digital platforms help companies stay in touch and introduce their work to new audiences, Landrum says meeting in person creates opportunities for deeper conversations. Discussions that begin with a question about a product can develop into a better understanding of a client's plans, challenges and priorities.

Meeting in person and making connections is a key part of the attractions business, believes the Chance team

Chance Rides also sees trade shows as a chance to reconnect with existing clients and industry peers, learn how requirements are changing, and gain insight into the direction of the amusement industry.

“These conversations help shape how we move forward,” says Landrum.

Chance Rides prepares for IAAPA Expo

For Chance Rides, attending industry events strengthens existing relationships while building new ones. The company views show season as an extension of online connections, offering a chance to put faces to names and continue conversations in person.

“Each show is an opportunity to strengthen existing relationships and begin new ones,” Landrum says.

The company will continue these conversations at IAAPA Expo, where visitors can meet the Chance Rides team at booth #S4826 to discuss projects, explore its offerings, and share their plans for the future.

“As the ways we connect continue to evolve, making time to show up, listen, and get to know one another remains a meaningful part of how we do business,” Landrum adds.

Last month, Chance Rides announced the appointment of Jayden Wallentine, who joined the company in April 2026 as a sales executive, managing its zoos and aquariums segment.

title: Game Volt receives 100 orders for social gaming attraction, Battle Arcade
summary:
Game Volt, the product division of CONDUCTR, the UK-based innovation studio, has already received 100 orders for the interactive gaming attraction, Battle Arcade, from customers throughout Europe, the US, and Canada.

Reflecting early operator confidence in the product, this milestone strengthens Game Volt’s position in the competitive socialising market.

Battle Arcade launched in August 2026. It is now live at several venues across North America and will make its playable IAAPA Expo debut in Orlando.

The product combines the proven operational systems and technology that power GameVolt’s wider product library, such as Supercharged Shuffleboard and The Arena, with a new platform. The result is a high-end visitor experience that is easy to operate.

Lauren Hatton, sales and partnerships manager (US) at Game Volt, says: "Operators want something that gets guests excited from the moment they see it, but they also need confidence in any experience after installation.

"Battle Arcade brings those priorities together: an experience people want to play from the moment they see it, backed by the technology and operational understanding we have developed across the Game Volt range.

"With Battle Arcade already live in North American venues, operators can see how it works in a real trading environment. Reaching 100 orders so soon after launch for a competitive socialising product is a strong endorsement of both the product and the team behind it."

Repeatable, responsive play

Developed for up to 10 players, Battle Arcade combines a high-resolution LED floor with colourful, fast-paced game worlds that visitors can explore without projection or wearables.

Short sessions, self-service operation, and an evolving content catalogue provide a versatile attraction that encourages repeat visits.

The platform is available in three configurations and offers opportunities for seasonal content, venue branding and licensed IP experiences.

"Battle Arcade’s full-colour LED floor gives us a much richer canvas for gameplay," says Matt Daly, head of partnerships (EMEA) at Game Volt.

"We can bring characters, environments and challenges to life beneath players’ feet, with visuals that guide the action and respond to every move.

"That capability also opens up exciting opportunities for licensed IP. We can build recognisable worlds into the experience and make them part of how people play. For operators, it means a versatile attraction with scope for new games, seasonal content and branded experiences that give guests fresh reasons to return.

"These orders across Europe, the US and Canada show the scale of the opportunity. Operators are investing in a premium competitive socialising experience, with the reassurance of proven systems and a partner that understands the demands of running a venue."

The momentum continues across the company's wider portfolio. Game Volt has also secured orders for its new socially connected midway gaming concept, Carnival Games, with its inaugural installation planned on a cruise ship in Q1 2027.

Delegates at IAAPA Expo 2026 in Orlando can learn more about Battle Arcade at Game Volt’s booth, #W1201. The team will be on hand to demonstrate the attraction's gameplay and discuss installation opportunities.

IAAPA Expo is taking place at the Orange County Convention Center (OCCC) in Orlando. Education sessions will be held from 16 to 19 November, with the show floor open from 17 to 20 November.

title: eatX - THE DARK RIDE DINING ATTRACTION
summary:
For decades, the leisure industry has treated dining and attractions as parallel tracks. Guests ride, then eat. They queue for a meal, then queue for a ride. The two have never truly occupied the same space - until now.


eatX is the world's first Dark Ride Dining Attraction: a fully patented, commercially deployable format in which the meal and the ride are the same experience. Guests board the FlowDiner - an autonomously moving, battery-powered dining vehicle developed and manufactured by MACK Rides - and travel as a group of up to four adults and two young children through a sequence of fully immersive themed environments. As they move, they eat. The story unfolds through projections, set design, lighting, soundscapes, and cuisine simultaneously. Nothing is supplementary. The food is not decoration for the ride, and the ride is not packaging for the food.


​A new product category


eatX does not sit within an existing attraction or dining typology. It is a hybrid format that creates its own category at the intersection of ride engineering, immersive storytelling and system gastronomy. This matters commercially because it addresses three pressures that operators across theme parks, resorts, FECs and arenas face simultaneously: limited available space, the demand for high-value guest experiences, and the need to grow revenue per square meter. eatX answers all three in a single footprint - using each square meter twice, as attraction space and as dining revenue space.

The FlowDiner vehicle took two years to develop. It travels at up to 0.5 metres per second, runs on an on-board electric drive, and operates as part of a trackless ride system - meaning the layout and narrative journey can be configured per operator and per IP. This adaptability is the platform's commercial engine: eatX is designed as a white-label concept, localisable for any brand, story or destination context.

​The first operator: Karls Erlebnis-Dorf


The proof of concept is already live. Karls Erlebnis-Dorf in Elstal, near Berlin Wall open the first eatX installation in summer 2027: the 'Strawberry Dining Journey'. The experience takes guests through five themed worlds across a three-course menu, built around the historically documented discovery of the garden strawberry in 1714. The narrative is grounded in Karls' brand DNA - family, farming, authenticity - and translated into a fully immersive production using projection, set construction, lighting design and choreographed cuisine. The story is the same for every guest; the memory is unique to each table.

​Built on proven foundations


eatX is not a concept born in a design studio. It emerges directly from operational experience. The MACK Group developed Eatrenalin - the Michelin-starred immersive fine-dining restaurant at Europa-Park Resort - as a prototype for the intersection of dining and storytelling. That real-world learning, combined with MACK Rides' century of engineering expertise and MACK One's role as the group's innovation and experience design engine, gave eatX an unusual starting point: deep technical credibility and demonstrated guest appetite, before the first commercial unit was built.

​Why this is innovation for the industry


The implications of eatX extend beyond a single attraction. For theme parks, it transforms underperforming or legacy spaces into high-value destinations. For resorts, it turns transitional dining into a central storytelling asset. For operators across formats - malls, FECs, stadia - it introduces a new anchor concept that drives dwell time, per-capita spend and social sharing from a single, compact footprint.

The format is scalable, brand-agnostic and operationally lean. System gastronomy ensures precision, throughput and quality without compromising the guest experience. The trackless vehicle system allows for flexible layout configuration per site. And the white-label model means the IP, the story and the brand identity belong entirely to the operator - eatX provides the engineering and the format.


Dining has always been the gap between two better things. eatX closes that gap permanently.

The food is not decoration for the ride, and the ride is not packaging for the food.


​A new product category


eatX does not sit within an existing attraction or dining typology. It is a hybrid format that creates its own category at the intersection of ride engineering, immersive storytelling and system gastronomy. This matters commercially because it addresses three pressures that operators across theme parks, resorts, FECs and arenas face simultaneously: limited available space, the demand for high-value guest experiences, and the need to grow revenue per square meter. eatX answers all three in a single footprint - using each square meter twice, as attraction space and as dining revenue space.

The FlowDiner vehicle took two years to develop. It travels at up to 0.5 metres per second, runs on an on-board electric drive, and operates as part of a trackless ride system - meaning the layout and narrative journey can be configured per operator and per IP. This adaptability is the platform's commercial engine: eatX is designed as a white-label concept, localisable for any brand, story or destination context.

​The first operator: Karls Erlebnis-Dorf


The proof of concept is already live. Karls Erlebnis-Dorf in Elstal, near Berlin Wall open the first eatX installation in summer 2027: the 'Strawberry Dining Journey'. The experience takes guests through five themed worlds across a three-course menu, built around the historically documented discovery of the garden strawberry in 1714. The narrative is grounded in Karls' brand DNA - family, farming, authenticity - and translated into a fully immersive production using projection, set construction, lighting design and choreographed cuisine. The story is the same for every guest; the memory is unique to each table.

​Built on proven foundations


eatX is not a concept born in a design studio. It emerges directly from operational experience. The MACK Group developed Eatrenalin - the Michelin-starred immersive fine-dining restaurant at Europa-Park Resort - as a prototype for the intersection of dining and storytelling. That real-world learning, combined with MACK Rides' century of engineering expertise and MACK One's role as the group's innovation and experience design engine, gave eatX an unusual starting point: deep technical credibility and demonstrated guest appetite, before the first commercial unit was built.

​Why this is innovation for the industry


The implications of eatX extend beyond a single attraction. For theme parks, it transforms underperforming or legacy spaces into high-value destinations. For resorts, it turns transitional dining into a central storytelling asset. For operators across formats - malls, FECs, stadia - it introduces a new anchor concept that drives dwell time, per-capita spend and social sharing from a single, compact footprint.

The format is scalable, brand-agnostic and operationally lean. System gastronomy ensures precision, throughput and quality without compromising the guest experience. The trackless vehicle system allows for flexible layout configuration per site. And the white-label model means the IP, the story and the brand identity belong entirely to the operator - eatX provides the engineering and the format.


Dining has always been the gap between two better things. eatX closes that gap permanently.
